name: Umar Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of employers, AI firms, unions, government and political groups, and we sell nothing. This interview is confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Umar Varga, 58, and I operate a drilling rig at a large mine. Before a shift I walk the machine, check the hoses and bit, then drill the pattern the survey team marked. I like solving a jam without losing half a day, but the noise follows me home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that work already?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI assistant every day to sort my shift notes and compare fault codes in the manual, though I make the call at the rig. My wife Leila runs a small bookshop, and our grown daughters have moved out. We have roughly three months of expenses saved, so my typical mine pay still carries most of the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the drill crew that a little help with the fault log is useful, even if the grand claims fade. I already use an AI assistant for the manuals every day. A machine can find the page faster than I can with dirty gloves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be pleased that my rig time and mine pay stay much the same. Leila’s bookshop has slow weeks, so I don’t call three months of savings comfortable. I would still try to make my notes cleaner because the next fitter needs to understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the normal drill pattern and continue checking the AI summary against the actual fault manual. This month I’d set aside one hundred from each pay if the shop takings allow it. During the first year of the small software changes, I’d add the fault code and my own observation to every handover note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be calm about my own shift. The screen would save a few minutes but would not choose where I place the bit. The shop’s uneven sales would remain the ordinary worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the assistant gets a code wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once caught it mixing up a hydraulic pressure warning with a temperature alarm. I went back to the manual and called the fitter before restarting, and I’d do the same again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put money away now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila’s shop had two thin months this autumn. I want the electricity bill covered without asking our daughters, even though both are earning for themselves.

say: I’d welcome **quicker fault logs** without claiming AI can drill for me.
I already use an **AI assistant** to search equipment manuals.
think: My **mine pay** looks steady while Leila’s bookshop still has thin months.
Three months of savings feels **limited** for our household.
do: Keep drilling the marked **rig pattern** and checking the manual.
Add my own **fault observations** to each handover during the first year.
Set aside **one hundred** per pay packet if shop takings permit.
feel: **Calm** about the rig, while mindful of uneven bookshop sales.
S0.quote: A machine can find the page faster than I can with dirty gloves.
fieldNote: Umar already uses an **AI assistant daily**, but he checks fault codes against the manual before making equipment decisions.

steps.text: Keep drilling the surveyed pattern and checking the manual
Use the AI assistant for fault notes and verify each code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew that dispatch and ordering will change before our drill bits do. I’d volunteer to test a new planning screen because I know where yesterday’s ground broke the neat pattern. Drivers and drillers should be in the mine’s planning trial, not just the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enjoy being useful in a trial, but I’d watch what happens to the survey and stores teams. If the mine trims those posts, it might expect my crew to absorb the checking. My own rig shifts probably remain for now; Leila’s shop could also face cheaper automated sellers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the survey lead next week to let me compare AI drill plans with the actual ground reports. I’d spend two evenings learning the planning screen with the crew’s trainer, then keep a record of unsafe suggestions. In the first year after the change, I’d still run the rig and send those examples back to the survey lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel curious and a bit uneasy. I like a tool that shows its working; I don’t like a target set by somebody who has never stood beside a jammed rig. The shop’s takings would keep me checking our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as an unsafe suggestion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan that puts a hole too close to an old void would be one. I’d mark the ground report that contradicts it and ask the survey lead to review the pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is this about protecting a desk job for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m not counting on a desk job. I want the people still operating rigs to have a say before the software becomes the only plan anyone sees.

say: I’d say **dispatch and ordering** change before the drill rig.
I’d ask for **operators** in the planning trial because we know the ground.
think: My rig shifts likely continue, but **survey cuts** could push checking onto my crew.
Cheaper automated sellers could squeeze **Leila’s shop** as well.
do: Ask the survey lead to compare **AI drill plans** with ground reports.
Learn the **planning screen** with the crew trainer over two evenings.
Run the rig and report **unsafe suggestions** during the first year.
feel: **Curious** about testing the tool and uneasy about remote targets and shop sales.
S1.quote: Drivers and drillers should be in the mine’s planning trial, not just the office.
fieldNote: Umar seeks a place in the **planning trial** because his knowledge of unstable ground can catch errors before drilling.
He expects continued rig work, yet **household income** could tighten if automated sellers hurt Leila’s small bookshop.

steps.text: Learn the AI drill planning screen with the crew trainer
Run the drill rig and report unsafe plan suggestions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 could replace much of the planning office, while the drilling robots arrive around 2031. The three-year gap before drilling robots arrive is time to earn, not proof that our rig jobs survive. I’d ask management what the trial machines actually cost and when they might order them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 60 at the AI date and 63 at the robot date. I’m good with equipment, but a robot that drills as well as a person would remove the reason to pay me to run the rig. Leila’s bookshop might lose sales sooner, and three months of bills would not carry both of us long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for the mine’s technician vacancy list and apply for one posted electrical maintenance trainee opening if I meet its requirements. I’d book an appointment with the bookshop accountant to see which expenses Leila and I can cut. In 2029 I’d still drill for pay if scheduled, and I’d try the remote monitoring system if the mine makes it available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, with that restless feeling before an unexpected breakdown. I have a few moves, but none guarantees a wage when robots reach the pit. I would not tell Leila that a new screen means I have secured another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a technician post survive capable robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. I’m asking for a real vacancy because it could keep me earning for a while, not because it is robot-proof. I’d read the contract before paying for any extra certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expenses would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would pause the shop’s planned new shelving and my weekend fishing trips. We would keep the electricity and stock bills current before buying anything decorative.

say: I’d tell the crew **planning AI** arrives in 2028 and drilling robots around 2031.
I’d ask management for actual **robot orders** and costs.
think: At **63**, a capable drilling robot could end the rig wages I expect.
Leila’s **shop income** may weaken sooner, and three months of bills is thin.
do: Apply for a posted **maintenance trainee** opening if qualified.
Review shop costs with the **accountant** and pause new shelving.
Keep drilling in **2029** if scheduled, and try remote monitoring if offered.
feel: **Anxious** about losing both income sources, though I still see possible moves.
S2.quote: The three-year gap before drilling robots arrive is time to earn, not proof that our rig jobs survive.
fieldNote: Umar separates the loss of **planning work in 2028** from the direct threat to his rig wages around 2031.
He explores a **real trainee opening** while admitting maintenance may also change under capable robots.

steps.text: Apply for a posted electrical maintenance trainee opening if qualified
Pause new bookshop shelving and weekend fishing trips
Keep drilling for pay in 2029 if scheduled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that 2031 gives us five years to test alternatives before thinking AI takes over the office. Drilling robots around 2034 would meet me at 66, which is near my hoped-for retirement but not a date I can bank on. I’d put the mine’s dates beside my own figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d prefer this warning to the fast one, because I can keep building savings while the rig needs me. Leila and I cannot assume the bookshop will fund retirement, and I have not checked what any pension would pay. A machine arriving at 66 could still force a finish before our bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request my pension statement and the mine’s retirement terms this month. I’d ask Leila to separate the shop account from our home bills so we can see what the shop actually contributes. During 2032 I’d keep taking rig shifts and apply for any open trainer role if I can show the younger crew the ground checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy but less rushed. I could work with a real five-year calendar and test whether teaching new starters suits me. I’d still want the mine to say plainly if the trainer job is only temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would training people make sense if rigs become automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might only be useful during the changeover. I would apply for an advertised role and ask its length rather than call it a retirement bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension statement is lower than you expect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would cut the bookshop expansion idea and keep my paid rig shifts longer if they exist. We would not ask our daughters to fill the gap.

say: I’d say **2031 AI** changes office work before drilling robots reach us around 2034.
I’d compare the mine’s **dates** with my household figures.
think: I can build **savings** while the rig still needs operators.
A forced finish at **66** could still come before our bills are covered.
do: Request a **pension statement** and written mine retirement terms.
Separate **shop accounts** from household bills with Leila.
Keep paid rig shifts in **2032** and apply for an open trainer role.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to test a plan over five years.
S3.quote: A machine arriving at 66 could still force a finish before our bills are covered.
fieldNote: Umar wants **pension figures** before treating age 66 as a safe stopping point; the bookshop is no guaranteed retirement income.
He sees a **trainer role** as possible paid work during transition, provided an actual opening exists and its term is clear.

steps.text: Keep paid drilling shifts during 2032 if available
Apply for an advertised mine trainer role and check its term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade of warning gives the mine time to put drivers and drillers in the machine trials. Full thinking AI in 2036 would take office tasks first; drilling robots around 2039 are the direct change for me. I’d want younger operators to learn how to question the machine before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 at the AI date and 71 at the robot date. I hope I’ll have retired before a robot drills my pattern, but hope is not a statement from the pension fund. The long lead time could let Leila and me decide whether the bookshop stays open for pleasure or has to earn its keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the pension provider for yearly projections and keep a shared account sheet with Leila. I’d continue paid drilling while it makes sense, save any spare wages, and mentor newer operators on ground reports if the mine gives me that work. In 2037 I’d review our income and, if the bills are covered, leave the rig on the retirement date we choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly calm about the technology reaching my own rig so late. I would still have to be honest about money and health each year. A long warning is useful only if we actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would mentoring include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show a new driller how to compare the survey marks with an old void map and when to stop the rig for a second look. That judgement can be written down while experienced people are still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you promise to leave the rig in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If our account sheet says we need the wages, I would ask for the work that remains and keep going if my health allows. I won’t dress a wish up as a pension.

say: I’d ask for **operator trials** during the long warning.
I’d teach newer drillers to **question plans** before I leave.
think: At **71** when drilling robots arrive, I hope to have retired but need pension figures.
Leila and I must decide whether the **bookshop** needs to earn income.
do: Request yearly **pension projections** and update our account sheet.
Continue paid drilling and **mentor operators** if the mine offers that work.
Review **2037 income** before choosing whether to leave the rig.
feel: **Calm** about a late robot date, while taking yearly money and health checks seriously.
S4.quote: I won’t dress a wish up as a pension.
fieldNote: Umar expects the **2039 robot date** after his preferred rig career, yet insists on checking pension and shop income.
His interest in **mentoring** comes from specific ground checks he wants younger operators to retain during machine trials.

steps.text: Continue paid drilling shifts while health and mine work permit
Save available wages after checking yearly pension projections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because a robot could be drilling at 63 while Leila’s shop is already having lean months. I’d want honest machine purchase dates, a chance at a real maintenance opening and clear terms if my rig job ends. Three months of savings means a rumour can change what we buy this week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who checks a plan when the person who wrote it is gone. I have stopped a rig over an old void that looked harmless on the drawing. If people leave before that knowledge is passed on, somebody will have to relearn it the hard way.

headlineQuote: Three months of savings means a rumour can change what we buy this week.
portrait: Umar, **58**, operates a mine drilling rig and checks plans against the ground before boring each pattern.
He uses an **AI assistant daily** for manuals and fault notes, but verifies its answers.
His mine wages carry a household with **uneven bookshop sales** and roughly three months of savings.
He tests new tools readily, while demanding **actual vacancies** and pension figures before changing course.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Umar most because drilling robots around 2031 could end his mine wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **purchase dates**, a real maintenance opening and clear exit terms if his rig job ends.
